name: Yusuf Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach geography at Kestrel Lane Academy, a secondary school in a small market town, and this is my second year. I'm in by half seven to photocopy before the queue builds, then it's five lessons, a break duty by the bike sheds, and usually a Year 9 group that tests me. I like the moment a kid finally gets why a river bends. I'm on a one-year contract that ends in July, so there's always that hum in the background.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The marking and the paperwork after the kids go home, honestly. I'm slower at it than the others in the department, and Mr Doyle, my head of department, has already said my feedback needs to be tighter. I live with my partner Ines, who's a care assistant, and we rent a flat above the bakery on Mill Street, so money's tight and we've got maybe two weeks' cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say in the staffroom: the shiny tools were never the problem, the problem is thirty kids in a room and not enough staff. Online I'd probably share something from the union about class sizes. I'm not going to cheer the fact that the hype died, I'd just say let's fix the basics now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI fizzling out doesn't save me. My contract still ends in July, and Kestrel Lane is running a budget deficit, so whether I stay has nothing to do with robots. The only small thing is that the marking tool I use now and then for quiz feedback stays a bit handy, and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and get my lesson observations up to a decent grade before spring, because that's what decides renewals. I'd join the union properly instead of just reading their emails, about twelve a month. And I'd look at the two other schools within a bus ride in case Kestrel Lane can't keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady but nervous, if that makes sense. Nothing dramatic changes in this picture, and that's almost the worry, because the problems I've already got just stay. Two weeks of savings doesn't feel like a cushion, it feels like a held breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the contract ends in July. What happens in your head when you picture that letter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a held breath, really. I picture Mr Doyle calling me into the office after period five, and I already know what his face looks like. AI going nowhere doesn't stop budget cuts from going somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the contract isn't renewed, what's the first thing you and Ines would cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car would go first, it's Ines's old hatchback and we barely need it. Then the gym and the streaming stuff. If I lose the contract at Kestrel Lane, the nearest other secondary posts are forty minutes away, so I'd probably end up on supply work, which pays by the day and dries up in summer.

say: I'd say the **real problem** in schools was never technology, it was too many kids and too few staff.
I'd share **union posts** about class sizes and funding rather than talk about AI at all.
think: I think AI fading changes nothing about my **one-year contract** ending in July.
I think the **budget deficit** at Kestrel Lane is a bigger threat to me than any software.
do: Get my **lesson observations** up to a good grade before the spring renewal talks.
Join the **union** properly and pay the twelve a month instead of just reading emails.
Check posts at the **two schools** a bus ride away in case Kestrel Lane can't keep me.
feel: He feels **steady but nervous**, because his existing worries simply stay in place.
His two weeks of savings feels like a **held breath**, not a cushion.
S0.quote: AI going nowhere doesn't stop budget cuts from going somewhere.
fieldNote: His fear in the calm picture is entirely about the **contract renewal**, not technology.
He moves from the **staffroom line** about funding to a private, personal dread of one meeting.
Thin savings and **few local posts** mean losing the job pushes him straight onto daily supply work.

steps.text: Push his lesson observation grades up before the spring contract review
Join the teachers' union and pay the monthly fee
Sell Ines's old hatchback if the contract isn't renewed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need rules, written with teachers, before any of this gets pushed into classrooms. With friends I'd say AI can draft a worksheet but it can't calm a kid who's crying in the corridor. Online I'd back the union asking for a say in how it's used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it worries me because the bit I'm worst at, the marking and planning, is exactly the bit software does well. If the academy trust buys a planning platform, they might decide one experienced teacher plus software can cover what two of us do. A junior on a one-year contract is the easiest person not to renew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the trust's training on whatever platform they pick in the first term, instead of avoiding it. I'd ask Mr Doyle to let me run the Year 8 mapping unit with the AI quiz tool so I've got something to show at renewal. And I'd start putting fifty a month aside, even if it means fewer takeaways with Ines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a knot in my stomach about the summer. I like the classroom part a lot, and that part doesn't go away. But I can see the academy trust's spreadsheet where my name is the cheapest one to drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your week would the software take first, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Report writing and marking, for sure, and lesson planning after that. Last term I spent most of a Sunday writing sixty Year 9 reports, and a tool could do the first draft in minutes. The kids still need someone stood at the front, but the trust might want fewer of us standing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI now and then. Would you be one of the people who learns it fast, or wait for others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm a wait-until-it's-proven person. I'd let Priya in maths try things first and then copy what works, which is what I did with the quiz tool last year. But in this picture I can't wait too long, because being the one who can't use the platform is a bad look on a short contract.

say: I'd say teachers need a **real say**, through the union, before AI tools get pushed into classrooms.
I'd tell friends software can draft a **worksheet** but it can't calm a crying kid in a corridor.
think: I think the **marking and planning** I'm slowest at is exactly what software does best.
I think a junior on a **one-year contract** is the easiest person for the trust not to renew.
do: Attend the trust's **platform training** in the first term instead of avoiding it.
Run the Year 8 **mapping unit** with the AI quiz tool to show something at renewal.
Put **fifty a month** aside by cutting takeaways with Ines.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, with a knot in his stomach about whether he's kept on in summer.
He still **loves the classroom** part, which he believes software can't replace.
S1.quote: I can see the academy trust's spreadsheet where my name is the cheapest one to drop.
fieldNote: His public line is about **teacher voice**; privately he sees himself as the cheapest cut.
He names **report writing** as the first task to go, from a very specific lost Sunday.
As a **wait-and-copy** adopter he knows waiting is risky on a short contract, so he moves early anyway.

steps.text: Attend the academy trust's planning platform training in the first term
Back the union's push for teacher say over classroom AI
Set aside fifty a month from takeaway money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that governments need to protect schools as places where kids are looked after by people, not just taught by screens. At work I'd push the union to get guarantees on staff numbers written down fast. Online I'd probably be angrier than I usually let myself be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished as a geography teacher within a couple of years. If a machine can explain plate tectonics better than me, mark every essay and plan every lesson, what's left for a junior who's still learning is mostly supervision. And supervision gets paid less than teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop thinking about the long career and get practical in the first six months. I'd ask about the pastoral side, being a head of year assistant or behaviour mentor, because that's people work. I'd also go to Ines's care home and ask what qualifications their activities coordinator needs, as a back-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. I only just got here after the degree and the training year, and the ladder would be pulled up before I climbed it. With two weeks of savings there's no gap year to work out who I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI comes in 2028 and robots about three years later. How does that split land on a teacher's day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking part goes in 2028, so planning, marking, explaining, all of it. The hands-on part of my job is crowd control, field trips, a hug when a kid's parents split, and robots for that don't come until about 2031. So I'd probably get three years as a sort of supervisor before even that's in question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What would you say to Ines the night you realised this was real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ines something strange that night. My partner Ines is a care assistant, and her job might actually be safer than mine for once. Care work is hands-on, so she'd have until the robots show up. Then we'd sit down with the bank app and work out how long her wage alone covers the rent on Mill Street.

say: I'd demand the government protect schools as places where kids are **cared for by people**.
I'd push the union to win **written guarantees** on staff numbers quickly.
think: I think I'm **finished** as a geography teacher within a couple of years.

S2.quote: My partner Ines is a care assistant, and her job might actually be safer than mine for once.
fieldNote: He sees the **thinking side** of teaching gone in 2028, leaving him a lower-paid supervisor.
The robot gap gives him **three years** of hands-on supervision work, not a career.
He reverses household roles in his head: **Ines's care job** becomes the safer income.

steps.text: Apply for a pastoral or head of year assistant role at Kestrel Lane
Press the union for written staffing guarantees
Plan to cover the rent on Ines's care wage if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same things, just calmer: we've got a few years, so let's use them to plan properly with teachers in the room. I'd be at union meetings asking for retraining money, not just protests. With mates I'd joke that at least I'll finish paying off the laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still the end of teaching as I trained for it, just with time to get through my induction and get a permanent post first. A permanent contract would make me harder to drop. So the next five years become a race to get as secure as possible before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd chase a permanent post, at Kestrel Lane or the other school on the bus route. I'd take the trust's free course on special educational needs support, because working one-to-one with kids who struggle feels like the last thing to go. And I'd start saving twenty a week into a separate pot Ines can't see me dipping into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less panicky, more grim. I've got time to do something about it, which is better than watching it happen. But I'd still look at every new teacher coming out of training and wonder why they bothered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you compared to the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the extra years let me get settled before the thinking side goes in 2031, and the robot side wouldn't come until around 2034. That's long enough to switch towards special needs and pastoral work, which is more hands-on. In the two-year picture I'd be scrambling; here I'd be steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Kestrel Lane would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, honestly, who's a maths teacher a year ahead of me, because she's great on a screen but hates the behaviour side. And the teaching assistants, because a lot of what they do is marking support and reading groups. Mrs Achebe, our longest-serving teaching assistant, has been there nineteen years and has nothing else lined up.

say: I'd tell colleagues we've got **a few years**, so plan properly with teachers in the room.
I'd ask the union for **retraining money**, not just protests.
think: I think it's still **the end of teaching** as I trained for it, just slower.
I think the next five years are a race to get a **permanent contract** before 2031.

Take the trust's free **special needs** support course in the first year.
Save **twenty a week** into a separate pot for when work changes.
feel: He feels **less panicky but grim**, glad of time but sure the job is changing.
He wonders why **new trainees** still bother joining the profession.
S3.quote: Mrs Achebe, our longest-serving teaching assistant, has been there nineteen years and has nothing else lined up.
fieldNote: The extra years shift him from **scrambling to steering**, towards special needs and pastoral work.
He worries most about **teaching assistants**, whose reading and marking support goes first.
A **permanent contract** becomes his main shield, more than any new skill.

steps.text: Apply for a permanent geography post on the local bus route
Take the academy trust's free special needs support course
Save twenty a week in a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse for leaving teachers in the dark. At work I'd want the union planning for it now. With friends I'd probably say it's far enough off that I'll worry about it once I've got a permanent job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is most of my early career, so it feels less like a threat and more like a slow tide. I'd probably have a permanent post and some experience by then, which counts for something. But I'd be about thirty-seven when thinking AI arrives, which is a hard age to start over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still take the special needs course, but without the panic, maybe next year. I'd use the AI planning tools now and then, the way colleagues do, so I'm not behind. And I'd push to get on the union's school committee so I'm in the room when the trust makes plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy, not frightened. Knowing thinking AI is ten years off is like knowing the flat will need a new boiler at some point. You don't lose sleep tonight, but you put a bit by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, where do you picture yourself in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably still at a school, but doing more of the pastoral and special needs side, maybe as a head of year. Geography lessons might be a screen with me walking round helping, a bit like a coach. I'd hope Ines and I have kids by then, which makes the money side scarier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lean towards unions and public support. What would you want the government doing over that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proper retraining funds for teachers and teaching assistants, paid for out of what the tech firms earn. A guarantee that every class still has a qualified adult in the room. And not leaving it to each academy trust to decide on its own, because ours would just pick the cheapest option.

I'd tell friends I'll worry about it once I've got a **permanent job**.
think: I think a decade feels like a **slow tide**, not a sudden threat.
I think starting over at **thirty-seven** would be hard, even with experience.
do: Take the **special needs course** next year without panic.
Use AI **planning tools** now and then so he isn't left behind colleagues.
Stand for the union's **school committee** to be in the room for trust plans.
feel: He feels **mostly uneasy**, like knowing a boiler will need replacing eventually.
S4.quote: Knowing thinking AI is ten years off is like knowing the flat will need a new boiler at some point.
fieldNote: With a decade, he expects to have a **permanent post** and some experience first.
He pictures teaching as **coaching around a screen**, with him doing pastoral work.
His policy ask is specific: **retraining funds** paid by tech firms and a qualified adult per class.

steps.text: Take the special needs support course next year
Use AI planning tools for some lessons each term
Stand for the union's school committee at Kestrel Lane

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because I'd lose the thinking side of teaching before I'd even finished learning it. What would help is a permanent contract, honestly, and a funded route into special needs or pastoral work that doesn't need me to quit and pay for a course. Teaching is the job I spent five years getting into, and I'd like the chance to keep some of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the kids. Everyone talks about teachers' jobs, but a fourteen-year-old with no adult who knows their name is the real loss. A machine can know a kid's test scores, but a teacher knows which kid hasn't had breakfast.

headlineQuote: A machine can know a kid's test scores, but a teacher knows which kid hasn't had breakfast.
portrait: Yusuf is a 27-year-old **second-year geography teacher** on a one-year contract at a small market-town academy.
He rents with Ines, a care assistant, and has about **two weeks** of savings.
He waits for others to prove tools first, but **moves early** when his contract depends on it.
He blames **budgets and trust managers** more than technology, and leans on the union.
His worry rises sharply with fast AGI, then eases to **unease** when there's a decade to prepare.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd lose the **thinking side** of teaching before learning it.
whatWouldHelp: A **permanent contract** would make him harder to drop.
A **funded route** into special needs or pastoral work, without paying for courses himself.
